aboutBiography: I am a Mechanical Engineering graduate from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET, CGPA 3.47/4.00; Senior Year Trend: L4/T1: 3.71, L4/T2: 3.96) with 8 years of combined academic & industry experience in computational modeling and utility-scale cyber-physical infrastructure.

My independent research and academic publications investigate how interpretable mathematical structure can be combined with modern machine learning and control. Recently, I implemented the SINDy-RL framework based on a paper titled 'SINDy-RL: Interpretable and Efficient Model-Based Reinforcement Learning' (Zolman et al., 2025) on the nonlinear CartPole swing-up control task—constructing a 41-term quadratic control-affine basis library via PySINDy (Sequential Thresholded Ridge Regression) and coupling the learned sparse surrogate model with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in Ray RLlib.

In parallel, as an Executive Engineer at Northern Electricity Supply PLC (2018–Present), I contributed to developing a utility-scale digital twin spanning ~2 million customer meters, ~20,000 km of distribution lines, and ~13,000 transformers, and independently architected full-stack Web and Mobile spatial sensing platforms using Python (Django REST Framework), PostgreSQL/PostGIS, and Flutter/Dart.

projects.title: SINDy-RL Cart-Pole: Implementation, Diagnostics & Learned-Model Simulation
projects.subtitle: Model-Based RL · Sparse System Identification · Dyna-Style PPO on dm_control Cart-Pole Swing-Up

galleryImages.caption: Figure 1: Dyna-style SINDy-RL closed-loop architecture, 14-term sparse learned discrete-time dynamics (update 39), and 40-update real vs. surrogate evaluation diagnostics.

projects.executiveSummary: An end-to-end reproduction and failure-mode diagnosis of Zolman et al. (2024), SINDy-RL, on the nonlinear dm_control cart-pole swing-up task. Built from scratch on a single laptop CPU using an ensemble of sparse polynomial models (PySINDy, 20 models, STLRidge) to learn discrete-time dynamics (Δt = 0.01 s) and reward from ~48k real environment steps (8k offline + 40 × 1k on-policy), while training a 2×64 tanh PPO policy inside the surrogate via Ray RLlib.
projects.problemStatement: Model-free RL (such as PPO) needs millions of environment interactions to swing up and balance a cart-pole from hanging down. SINDy-RL replaces the real environment with a tiny, human-readable set of polynomial equations fit from only a few thousand real steps, then trains PPO entirely inside that learned model. However, during Dyna-style training, real returns peak at 610.2 (update 25, inside the paper’s 600–650 band) before oscillating between 250 and 610—raising a fundamental scientific question: is the learned SINDy dynamics model degrading, or is policy optimization exploiting surrogate drift?
projects.methodologyArchitecture:
1. Sparse Dictionary & Ensemble STLRidge (Δt = 0.01 s): Formulated a 41-term quadratic control-affine candidate library Θ(x, u) over state x = [x, cos θ, sin θ, ẋ, θ̇] and scalar force u (205 possible terms across 5 state equations). Fitted a 20-model bagged ensemble via Sequential Thresholded Ridge Regression (STLRidge, threshold = 0.005, α = 0.05), pruning the dynamics down to 14 non-zero terms (93.2% sparse) and reward to 5 terms.
2. Surrogate-Guided Ray RLlib PPO: Trained a 2×64 tanh MLP policy with PPO entirely inside the learned SINDy world model (70k surrogate steps per Dyna iteration; 2.8M total surrogate steps vs. 48k real steps), collecting 1,000 on-policy real steps per update and clipping out-of-bounds trajectories (|x| > 2 or |v| > 10).
3. Controlled 6-Hypothesis Diagnostic Investigation: Executed targeted experiments isolating dynamics refit collapse, policy drift / model exploitation, off-policy buffer pollution, reward model collapse, control-authority loss, and single-seed variance.
projects.experimentalValidation: Across 40 Dyna updates (~48k real steps), the learned 14-term model matched true dm_control control-gain terms within ≤ 4% error (cart acceleration at θ=0: +0.0970 vs +0.0990 true; pole angular acceleration at θ=0: −0.1354 vs −0.1408 true; at θ=π: +0.1354 vs +0.1408 true). Controlled diagnostics proved that freezing dynamics after update 14 did not eliminate return drops—confirming that late-training oscillation stems from PPO policy drift over 70k surrogate steps per update rather than SINDy dynamics degradation.

equations.title: Learned 14-Term Discrete-Time SINDy Dynamics (Update 39, Δt = 0.01 s, 93.2% Sparse)
equations.explanation: Exact median ensemble coefficients recovered at Update 39 from 41 candidate terms per equation (205 total), retaining only 14 active terms. Note how cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 folds the cart control gain into 0.0970·u at θ=0 (true: 0.0990·u).

equations.title: Learned 5-Term Sparse Surrogate Reward Function (of 15 Candidates)
equations.explanation: Captures upright preference (+cos θ, +cos²θ) and penalties on cart position (−x²) and angular velocity (−θ̇²), fitted via 20-model ensemble STLRidge.

galleryImages.caption: Figure 1: Two-zone spark-ignition engine combustion simulation comparing 5 heat transfer models (Annand, Woschni, Modified Woschni, Hohenberg, Han et al.) against Rakopoulos [8] experimental data.

projects.executiveSummary: A comparative numerical study of five empirical convective heat transfer models—Annand (1963), Woschni (1967), Modified Woschni (Finol & Robinson), Hohenberg (1979), and Han et al. (1997)—in a two-zone spark-ignition (SI) engine cycle simulation written in MATLAB (ODE23, 1° crank-angle step). Simulated cylinder pressure, burned/unburned zone temperatures, cumulative work, heat flux, and piston-ring blow-by leakage were benchmarked against experimental pressure measurements by Rakopoulos [8] and evaluated across varying fuels (Gasoline, Methanol), equivalence ratios (φ = 0.8, 1.0, 1.2), engine speeds (3000–3500 rpm), and spark advances (0°–40°).
projects.problemStatement: Heat transfer from cylinder walls is a major factor governing internal combustion engine performance, exhaust emissions, cooling system design, and thermally induced mechanical stresses. Because a single empirical correlation rarely predicts heat flux accurately across all strokes of the engine cycle, engine modelers need a rigorous two-zone comparative analysis against experimental cylinder pressure traces to determine which heat transfer correlation performs best during compression, combustion, and expansion.
projects.methodologyArchitecture:
1. Two-Zone Closed Thermodynamic Cycle (IVC to EVO): Formulated the First Law of Thermodynamics following Ferguson [1] by splitting the cylinder mixture into burned (T_b) and unburned (T_u) zones sharing uniform pressure P(θ), coupled with a Wiebe burn-rate law (b = 5, n = 3, θ_s = -30°) and exponential piston-ring blow-by mass loss (C_blow_by = 1.1).
2. Five Heat Transfer Correlations in MATLAB ODE23: Implemented Annand (a = 0.5, b = 0.7), Woschni (C₁ = 2.28, C₂ = 3.24×10⁻³), Modified Woschni (characteristic height L(t) = 4V/πd_p², α = 1000), Hohenberg (instantaneous volume V^(-0.06), C₁ = 130, C₂ = 1.4), and Han et al. (C₁ = 687, C₂ = 0.494, C₃ = 7.3×10⁻⁷, k = 1.35) using a 1° step size in MATLAB ODE23 (Bore B = 3 inch, Stroke = 35/8 inch, ε = 0.25, T_wall = 420 K, T₁ = 310 K, P₁ = 101.325 kPa).
3. Experimental Validation & Parametric Sweeps: Benchmarked P–θ and P–V indicator diagrams against experimental measurements by Rakopoulos [8], and tested sensitivity across Methanol (φ = 1.0, 3000 rpm), Gasoline (φ = 0.8 at 3000 rpm; φ = 1.2 at 3500 rpm), and spark advance angles (0° to 40°).
projects.experimentalValidation: Published in Proceedings of the International Conference on Mechanical, Industrial and Energy Engineering (ICMIEE-PI-160369, Dec 26–27, 2016, Khulna, Bangladesh). Comparison against Rakopoulos [8] experimental pressure traces established stage-specific model recommendations: (1) Hohenberg model is closest to experimental data during the compression stage; (2) Han et al. and Woschni models bracket experimental peak pressure best during the combustion stage (where Annand overpredicts heat flux and underpredicts pressure, while Hohenberg overpredicts peak pressure); and (3) Modified Woschni and Annand models match experimental data best during the expansion stage.

projects.executiveSummary: Contributed to developing a utility-scale electrical distribution digital twin encompassing ~2 million customer meters, ~20,000 km of lines, and ~13,000 distribution transformers. Independently designed and deployed a production-grade Web GIS visualization platform and an offline-capable Flutter/Dart Mobile field-surveying system backed by Python (Django REST Framework) and PostgreSQL/PostGIS to map complete source-to-meter power connectivity and optimize network operations via load-flow and short-circuit simulations.
projects.problemStatement: Managing a regional distribution utility serving ~2 million consumers suffers from incomplete topological records between 33/11 kV substations, 11/0.4 kV distribution transformers, and end-user meters. Without an accurate, spatially synchronized digital twin, engineers cannot reliably compute feeder voltage drops, locate technical losses, evaluate short-circuit fault currents, or plan phase-balancing and transformer upgrades.
projects.methodologyArchitecture:
1. Spatial Graph Database & REST Backend: Architected a relational-spatial database in PostgreSQL/PostGIS with a Django REST Framework API modeling hierarchical source-to-meter connectivity (Substation → 11 kV Feeder → Distribution Transformer → Pole → Consumer Meter).
2. Offline Field Sensing & Mobile Synchronization: Independently built a cross-platform Flutter/Dart mobile surveying application enabling field engineers to capture GPS coordinates, meter telemetry, and pole-to-pole connectivity offline with conflict-free spatial synchronization.
3. Computational Load-Flow & Reliability Simulation: Integrated network asset data into computational engineering solvers (WindMil / Milsoft) to execute steady-state load-flow simulations, short-circuit current evaluations, and transformer reliability analyses.
projects.experimentalValidation: Deployed in production across the Northern Electricity Supply PLC distribution network (~20,000 km of lines and ~13,000 transformers). Enabled complete source-to-meter tracing for ~2 million customer meters, supporting data-driven feeder reconfiguration, voltage profile regulation, and capital asset planning.

galleryImages.caption: Figure 1: Sensor-instrumented rotating pharmaceutical production machinery monitoring Operating Hours, Temperature, Vibration, Pressure, Humidity, and Load for Hybrid RF-ANN predictive maintenance.

projects.executiveSummary: Presents a hybrid machine learning framework for predictive maintenance using 5,000 sensor-based operational records collected from rotating production equipment in a pharmaceutical manufacturing line (4,772 normal operation records and 228 failure records across 6 sensor variables: Operating Hours, Temperature, Vibration, Pressure, Humidity, and Load). A Random Forest model first analyzes feature importance, followed by a 32-neuron ReLU Artificial Neural Network (ANN) trained on an 80–20 split to predict failure probabilities and drive a three-state maintenance decision rule (Normal, Warning, Maintenance Required).
projects.problemStatement: Unexpected equipment failures in smart manufacturing environments cause unplanned downtime, high repair costs, and supply-chain disruptions. Reactive maintenance repairs equipment only after breakdown, while fixed-interval preventive maintenance causes unnecessary interventions. Relying on a single machine learning algorithm often limits interpretability and robustness across noisy, multi-variable industrial operating conditions with severe class imbalance (only 4.56% failure events).
projects.methodologyArchitecture:
1. Sensor Data Collection & Preprocessing (N = 5,000): Recorded 6 operational parameters—Operating Hours (mean 4015.54 ± 2279.87 hrs), Temperature (71.92 ± 11.15 °C), Vibration (3.20 ± 1.10 mm/s), Pressure (31.04 ± 5.46 bar), Humidity (45.89 ± 8.89%), and Load (67.33 ± 18.73%)—with binary failure labels (4,772 Normal = 0; 228 Failure = 1). Inspected for missing entries, normalized numerical features, and partitioned via an 80%–20% train-test split (4,000 train / 1,000 test).
2. Hybrid Random Forest + ANN Architecture: Applied Random Forest across decision trees to rank feature importance, then trained a feed-forward Artificial Neural Network (1 hidden layer with 32 ReLU neurons, sigmoid output layer, Adam optimizer with learning rate = 0.001 for 50 epochs) to output failure probability P(Failure) = g(f_RF(X)).
3. Three-State Maintenance Decision Rule: Classified machine operating conditions using empirical probability thresholds θ₁ = 0.3 and θ₂ = 0.6 into Normal (P < 0.3), Warning (0.3 ≤ P < 0.6), and Maintenance Required (P ≥ 0.6).
projects.experimentalValidation: Published in Proceedings of the 9th European International Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management (IEOM, Barcelona, Spain, July 20–22, 2026; DOI: 10.46254/EU09.20260000). Random Forest feature importance revealed that Load Percentage (0.2116) and Operating Hours (0.2044) are the primary drivers of machine failure, followed by Vibration (0.1827), Pressure (0.1655), Temperature (0.1501), and Humidity (0.0857). On the 1,000-record unseen test set, the hybrid model achieved 84.5% overall classification accuracy (836 True Negatives, 119 False Positives, 36 False Negatives, 9 True Positives; Precision = 0.0703, Recall = 0.20, F1-score = 0.104), and the study formulates SMOTE/cost-sensitive extensions to address the 4.56% rare-failure class imbalance.

publications.title: Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Predictive Maintenance in Smart Manufacturing Using Sensors
publications.authors: Sk. Humain Ahmed, Debashish Debnath, Bishwajit Saha, Ashraful Alam Limon, and Md. Nasif Hasan
publications.venue: Proceedings of the 9th European International Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management (IEOM), Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain, July 20–22, 2026
publications.abstract: Predictive maintenance has become an essential component of smart manufacturing systems for reducing unexpected equipment failures and improving operational efficiency. This study presents a hybrid machine learning framework for predictive maintenance using sensor-based machine operational data. The dataset consists of 5,000 machine operating records collected from sensor monitoring systems, including parameters such as operating hours, temperature, vibration, pressure, humidity, and machine load. A Random Forest model is first applied to analyze feature importance and identify the most influential parameters associated with machine failure. Subsequently, an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model is employed to predict machine failure conditions based on the selected operational features. The dataset is divided into training and testing subsets using an 80–20 split to evaluate the predictive capability of the model. Experimental results indicate that load percentage and operating hours are the most influential factors affecting machine failure, followed by vibration and pressure. The proposed framework achieved an overall prediction accuracy of 84.5%. Although failure events represent a small portion of the dataset, the developed system demonstrates the capability to identify potential machine degradation patterns and support data-driven maintenance planning. The results highlight the potential of hybrid machine learning approaches for improving predictive maintenance decision-making in smart manufacturing environments.

publications.title: Study and Simulation of Various Heat Transfer Models of SI Engine
publications.authors: Md Shariful Islam, Sk Humain Ahmed, and Afsar Ahammed
publications.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Mechanical, Industrial and Energy Engineering (ICMIEE-PI-160369), 26–27 December, 2016, Khulna, Bangladesh
publications.abstract: Heat transfer from cylinder walls is a major factor for engine performance, emission and the efficient design of cooling system of internal combustion engines. Furthermore, heat transfer phenomenon causes thermally induced mechanical stresses compromising the reliability of engine components. The ability to predict heat transfer in engines plays an important role in engine development and it’s cooling. Today, predictions are increasingly being done with numerical simulations. These methods are based on the principles of heat transfer. This paper shows a comparative study of different heat transfer models of SI engine. MATLAB programming was used here to simulate the various performance parameters of an SI engine to find the best possible model. To understand which model works better in which region of engine cycle various comparisons have been depicted graphically with available experimental results. Furthermore, some justifications of the simulations were made by showing results for different set of engine parameters.
